name: LM2576SX-5.0_NOPB
title: 3 A step-down switching regulator, 52 kHz, fixed 3.3/5/12/15 V or adjustable, 40 V (HV: 60 V) input

source.revision: SNVS107C, June 1999, revised April 2013 (package addendum 27 August 2015)

summary: The LM2576 is a monolithic buck regulator with a 3 A bipolar output switch, a 52 kHz fixed-frequency oscillator, a 1.23 V reference and internal loop compensation, so a working converter needs only an inductor, a catch diode and two capacitors. It comes in fixed 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and 15 V versions and an adjustable one, runs from up to 40 V in (60 V for the LM2576HV), and has cycle-by-cycle current limit, thermal shutdown, frequency foldback under overload and an active-high ON/OFF input with 50 µA standby current. It can also be wired as an inverting buck-boost or a negative boost. Packages are a 5-lead TO-220 and the 5-lead DDPAK/TO-263; the LM2576SX-5.0/NOPB is the 5 V, 40 V part in DDPAK/TO-263 on 500-piece reels.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input for the regulator and for the collector of the 3 A output switch. Bypass it to ground close to the part with an electrolytic of at least 100 µF.

pins.name: OUTPUT
pins.function: Emitter of the internal switch; the switching node. It drives the inductor and the cathode of the catch diode. Rated to −1 V to ground, steady state.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground. On both packages the mounting tab is the same lead frame as this pin, so either can carry the ground connection.

pins.name: FEEDBACK
pins.function: Output sense. On fixed versions it goes straight to the regulated output and feeds an internal divider; on the adjustable version it is the 1.23 V error-amplifier input from an external divider.

pins.name: ON/OFF
pins.function: Shutdown, active high. Low (0 V or a TTL low) runs the regulator; a TTL or CMOS high puts it into standby at 50 µA typical. It may be tied to VIN directly; it must not float.

circuits.title: Fixed 5 V, 3 A buck (Figure 1)
circuits.description: The basic step-down converter for the fixed versions, shown with the 5.0 V part, from an unregulated 7 V to 40 V supply (60 V for the HV part) to a 5 V rail at up to 3 A. While the switch is on, OUTPUT drives the 100 µH inductor from VIN; while it is off, the 1N5822 Schottky carries the inductor current from ground. FEEDBACK senses the output directly through the internal divider. ON/OFF is grounded so the regulator always runs. CIN is the input electrolytic, COUT the output filter that also sets the loop's pole pair with L1.

parts.value: 7 V to 40 V unregulated input (60 V for HV)

circuits.title: Test circuit, fixed output versions (Figure 21)
circuits.description: The circuit in which the fixed versions' system parameters and typical curves are measured. It is the basic buck with an MBR360 Schottky and a load across the output. The heavy-current loops (CIN, the GND pin, D1 and COUT) return to one ground point, and those leads are to be kept short.

circuits.title: Test circuit, adjustable version (Figure 22)
circuits.description: The adjustable version's measurement circuit, set to 5.00 V from a 7 V to 60 V input. R2 from the output to FEEDBACK over R1 to ground sets VOUT = 1.23 V × (1 + R2/R1); with 6.12k and 2k this gives 5.00 V. Everything else matches the fixed test circuit.

parts.value: 7 V to 60 V unregulated DC input

circuits.title: Inverting buck-boost, −12 V at 0.7 A (Figure 28)
circuits.description: A 12 V fixed part makes −12 V from a positive +12 V to +45 V input. The regulator's GND pin sits on the negative output and FEEDBACK goes to system ground, so the part regulates the 12 V between them. The inductor runs from OUTPUT to system ground; the 1N5822 conducts from the −12 V rail back to the switching node while the switch is off, and COUT sits between ground and −12 V. Up to about 0.7 A is available with 12 V or more in.
notes: For a −12 V output the input is limited to +28 V on the LM2576 and +48 V on the LM2576HV.

circuits.title: Negative boost, −5 V to −12 V in, −12 V out (Figure 29)
circuits.description: A negative input of −5 V to −12 V is boosted to a regulated −12 V. VIN and FEEDBACK are tied to system ground, and GND with ON/OFF rides on the −12 V output. The 100 µH inductor runs from the negative input to OUTPUT; the switch charges it from ground, and when the switch opens the 1N5820 passes its current from the −12 V rail into the switching node. Typical load: 400 mA at −5.2 V in, 750 mA at −7 V in; a heat sink may be needed.
notes: An input more negative than −12 V lets the output follow it past −12 V without harm to the regulator. A boost converter cannot limit current into a shorted load; a fuse or similar is needed for that.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for the buck circuit (Figure 30)
circuits.description: Holds the regulator in standby until the input rises past VTH ≈ VZ1 + 2 VBE(Q1). Below that, Z1 does not conduct, Q1 is off and the 20k pull-up drives ON/OFF high (off). Above it, current through R1 and Z1 into R2 turns Q1 on, which pulls ON/OFF low and lets the regulator run. Only the input side is shown: OUTPUT and FEEDBACK connect to the rest of the buck converter.

parts.value: to the inductor and catch diode

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for the buck-boost circuit (Figure 31)
circuits.description: The same lockout applied to the inverting buck-boost: the threshold network and Q1 return to the regulator's GND pin, which is the negative output rail, while CIN returns to system ground. Q1 pulls ON/OFF down to that rail once the input passes VZ1 + 2 VBE. Only the input side is shown; the rest is the inverting circuit.

parts.value: to the inductor and catch diode

circuits.title: Delayed start-up (Figure 32)
circuits.description: CD from VIN to ON/OFF with RD from ON/OFF to ground: when the input steps up, CD pulls ON/OFF high (standby) and then charges through RD until ON/OFF falls low enough for the regulator to start. With 20 V in and 0.1 µF with 47k the delay is about 10 ms; a longer RC gives a longer delay, but too long a time constant lets 60 Hz or 120 Hz input ripple reach ON/OFF. Only the input side is shown.

parts.value: to the inductor and catch diode

circuits.title: 1.2 V to 55 V adjustable 3 A supply with low output ripple (Figure 33)
circuits.description: An adjustable buck from a 55 V unregulated input on the HV adjustable part. L1 (150 µH), the 1N5822 and a 2000 µF output capacitor form the converter; R1 (1.21k) and the 50k variable resistor R2 set VOUT = 1.23 V × (1 + R2/R1). An optional second LC stage, 20 µH and 100 µF, after the feedback point reduces ripple at the output tenfold or better.

operation.text: An internal regulator powers a 1.23 V band-gap reference, a fixed-gain error amplifier, a 52 kHz oscillator and a PWM comparator whose output, gated with reset, thermal-shutdown and current-limit signals, drives the 3 A output switch between VIN and OUTPUT. The FEEDBACK pin feeds the error amplifier through an internal divider on the fixed versions (R1 = 1.0k with R2 of 1.7k, 3.1k, 8.84k or 11.3k for 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and 15 V); on the adjustable version R1 is open and R2 is 0 Ω. Loop compensation is internal.

Fixed outputs of 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and 15 V, and an adjustable version from 1.23 V to 37 V (57 V on the HV parts). Output tolerance is ±4 % over the specified line and load range and oscillator tolerance ±10 %. LM2576 parts run to 40 V in, LM2576HV parts to 60 V.

The switch limits current cycle by cycle (5.8 A typical) and the die has thermal shutdown. If a short or overload drags the output about 40 % below nominal, the oscillator drops to about 11 kHz and the minimum duty cycle from 5 % to about 2 %, lowering dissipation.

Ground ON/OFF, or drive it with a TTL low (typically under 1.6 V), for normal running. A TTL or CMOS high puts the part in standby, drawing 50 µA typical (200 µA maximum). The pin can be connected straight to +VIN with no series resistor, and is never to be left open.

Fast current edges in wiring inductance make voltage spikes, so the input capacitor, GND pin, catch diode and output capacitor loops are wired short and returned to a single ground point or a ground plane. Ground connections carrying power current need low impedance. On the TO-220 and DDPAK/TO-263 the tab and pin 3 are one lead frame and either may be used. On the adjustable version the divider resistors sit next to the regulator to keep the feedback trace short.
On the fixed versions FEEDBACK is wired to the output voltage point. On the adjustable version both divider resistors go near the part; resistors above 100 kΩ pick up more noise.

VIN needs at least a 100 µF electrolytic, with short leads, close to the regulator, for stability. Below −25°C electrolytics lose capacitance and gain ESR, so more capacitance may be needed; a ceramic or solid tantalum in parallel improves stability in the cold. For long life its RMS ripple current rating should exceed 1.2 × (tON/T) × ILOAD.

The selection guides (Figures 23 to 27) give inductors for continuous conduction, with peak-to-peak ripple about 20 % to 30 % of the maximum DC current. At light load the converter goes discontinuous, which is acceptable; below roughly 300 mA a deliberately discontinuous design allows a smaller inductor. The inductor must suit 52 kHz and carry 1.15 × ILOAD; past its rated current it saturates, its inductance collapses and the switch current climbs fast. Bobbin cores are cheapest but radiate more flux than closed cores, which can disturb nearby circuits and scope readings.

In continuous mode the inductor current is a triangle or sawtooth whose peak-to-peak size is fixed by VIN and VOUT; its average equals the load current, so it moves up and down with load. When the load falls far enough the valley reaches zero and the converter turns discontinuous, whatever the inductance.

COUT filters the output and sets the loop's dominant pole pair with the inductor. A value of 100 µF to 470 µF suits stable operation with ripple near 1 % of VOUT, with a voltage rating of at least 1.5 × VOUT; higher-voltage electrolytics usually have lower ESR. Ripple is ΔIIND × ESR: 220 µF to 1000 µF typically give 50 mV to 150 mV, larger values 20 mV to 50 mV, and low-ESR types 10 mV to 20 mV. In continuous mode an ESR under 0.03 Ω can make the regulator unstable, so a tantalum alone needs care; a tantalum making up 10 % to 20 % of the total beside aluminum helps at low temperature. Its 52 kHz ripple current rating needs a 50 % margin over the peak-to-peak inductor ripple. Typical aluminum electrolytics of 100 µF to 1000 µF have 0.5 Ω to 0.1 Ω ESR; low-ESR grades are under 0.15 Ω.

The diode carries the inductor current while the switch is off and goes close to the part with short leads. Schottky diodes give the best efficiency, especially below 5 V out. Soft-recovery fast diodes work; abrupt-recovery types can cause instability and EMI, and 60 Hz rectifiers such as the 1N4001 or 1N5400 are unsuitable. Its current rating should be at least 1.2 × the maximum load, or the full switch current limit if the supply must survive a sustained short, and its reverse rating at least 1.25 × the maximum input.

The output carries a sawtooth at the switching frequency, typically about 1 % of VOUT, plus short spikes at the sawtooth peaks from the switch edges and the capacitor's inductance (ESL). Low-inductance capacitors with short leads reduce the spikes. A small extra LC filter of 20 µH and 100 µF after the output can reduce ripple and spikes about tenfold.

Estimate PD, multiply by θJA (or by θJC + interface + heat sink) for the temperature rise, add the highest ambient, and compare with a target about 15°C below the 125°C maximum junction temperature; if it is higher, a heat sink, or a better one, is needed. A DDPAK/TO-263 sheds heat into board copper: θJA is 50°C/W with 0.5 in², 37°C/W with 1 in² and 32°C/W with 1.6 in² or more.

For 5 V out, 15 V maximum in and 3 A: the 5 V selection guide gives region L100, a 100 µH inductor (AIE 415-0930, Pulse PE92108 or Renco RL2444); COUT 680 µF to 2000 µF aluminum electrolytic rated 20 V; a 20 V, 3 A Schottky such as 1N5823 or SR302; and a 100 µF, 25 V aluminum electrolytic at the input and ground pins.

For 10 V out, 25 V maximum in, 3 A and 52 kHz: R1 = 1k and R2 = 7.15k; E·T = 115 V·µs, region H150, a 150 µH inductor (AIE 415-0936, Pulse PE-53115 or Renco RL2445); COUT 680 µF electrolytic rated at least 15 V; a 30 V, 3.3 A Schottky such as 31DQ03; and a 100 µF aluminum electrolytic at the input.

With GND on the negative output and FEEDBACK grounded, a fixed part regulates a negative rail. The regulator sees the sum of input and output magnitudes, so for −12 V out the input is limited to +28 V (LM2576) or +48 V (LM2576HV). Switch currents are higher than in a buck, so less output current is available: about 700 mA at 12 V or more in, and at light load the input can fall to about 4.7 V. The start-up input current is also higher and can trip a source limited below 5 A; a delayed turn-on or undervoltage lockout lets the input rise first. The buck procedure does not apply: inductors of 68 µH to 220 µH are recommended, and the output capacitor must be larger than for a buck, reaching thousands of µF at low input or high load.
Switch current is high in a boost, most of all at low input, and the switch rating sets the load limit. A boost cannot protect a shorted load, so a fuse or other means may be needed.
